MetaPointFinder: Detection of Antimicrobial Resistance -1 
Conferring Point Mutations (ARMs) from Metagenomic Reads  2 
Aldert L. Zomer1,2, Sam Nooij1, Cailean Carter3,4, Alison E. Mather3,4,5† 3 
1 Department of Biomolecular Health Sciences, Faculty of Veterinary Medicine, Utrecht 4 
University, the Netherlands  5

Resistance from a One Health Perspective / WOAH Reference Laboratory for 7 
Campylobacteriosis, Utrecht, the Netherlands 8 
3Quadram Institute Bioscience, Norwich Research Park, Norwich, NR4 7UQ, UK 9

†Corresponding author: [alison.mather@quadram.ac.uk] 12 
Abstract 13 
Background: Many clinically important antimicrobial resistance (AMR) phenotypes such as 14 
fluoroquinolones and rifamycins are driven by antimicrobial resistance -conferring mutations 15 
(ARMs) in conserved chromosomal loci (e.g., gyrA, parC, rpoB). Resistome profiling by 16 
metagenomics sequencing is often proposed as an ideal AMR surveillance tool as it is organism -17 
agnostic, but currently, existing metagenomic AMR surveillance pipelines are only able to identify 18 
acquired AMR genes but not point mutations associated with AMR. This is a serious gap in 19 
metagenomics-based AMR surveillance, as the true extent of AMR may be underestimated.  20 
Methods: We developed MetaPointFinder (v1), a read-based method that can process both long 21 
and short metagenomic reads. The tool identifies resistance -determining regions in reads using 22 
DIAMOND (translated protein) and KMA (nucleotide), and classifies known resistant versus wild-23 
type variants by aligning the sequences using pwalign and assessing the observed mutations 24 
based on known resistance mutations in the AMRFinderPlus database. The tool outputs ARMs per 25 
read, per gene and per antibiotic class.  26 
Results: In proof -of-concept analyses, MetaPointFinder identified known AMR -associated 27 
mutations and quantified resistant/susceptible read counts and ratios from metagenomic 28 
samples with corroborating phenotypic resistance data when available. We benchmark our tool 29 
using simulated reads from DNA and from reverse-translated protein references with read lengths 30 
of 100–5000 bp and error rates between 0 and 30%, simulating both Illumina and Nanopore error 31 
rates. We show that MetaPointFinder outperforms any available method for detection of ARMs 32 
in metagenomics data.  33 
Conclusion: MetaPointFinder complements gene -centric resistome profiling by capturing 34 
chromosomal mutation-based AMR directly from metagenomes. 35

Impact Statement 36 
Many clinically important antimicrobial resistance (AMR) phenotypes such as fluoroquinolones 37 
and rifamycins are driven by antimicrobial resistance -conferring mutations (ARMs) in conserved 38 
chromosomal loci (e.g., gyrA, parC, rpoB). Resistome profiling by metagenomic sequencing is ideal 39 
for AMR surveillance, but existing pipelines detect only acquired genes and ignore point 40 
mutations. MetaPointFinder bridges this gap.  The tool accurately identifies reads carrying 41 
resistance-determining regions using DIAMOND (protein) and KMA (DNA), aligns them, and 42 
classifies resistant versus wild -type variants using known mutations from the AMRFinderPlus 43 
database. 44 
Introduction 45 
Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a threat to human and animal health globally, and the rapid and 46 
accurate quantification of AMR is critical to any strategy to reduce its burden. Generation and 47 
availability of bacterial sequence data and lower costs compared to phenotypic antibiotic 48 
susceptibility testing makes genotypic prediction of AMR increasingly common. Many tools exist 49 
that facilitate the prediction of AMR from genome sequences such as ResFinder [1], 50 
AMRFinderPlus [2] or RGI [3]. Most available tools predict resistance from both acquired 51 
antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) , and from antimicrobial resistance mutations (ARMs) in 52 
resistance-determining regions (RDRs) which are often found in essential genes. The identification 53 
of genotypic resistance does not necessarily equate to phenotypic resistance, but concordance 54 
between phenotype and genotype is generally fairly high [4–7]. Whole genome -based AMR 55 
surveillance requires culturing of isolates  and this restricts the assessment of AMR to specific 56 
targeted bacteria. An organism -agnostic alternative which does not require culturing is 57 
metagenomic sequencing, where estimation of the resistome can be obtained either by mapping 58 
reads to ARG databases or by assembling metagenomic reads into contigs and looking for ARGs 59 
in the assemblies [8–10]. 60 
Metagenomic sequencing has transformed ARG profiling, as it offers a more complete overview 61 
of the types and diversity of ARGs within samples. It has been applied in a variety of different 62 
settings across the One Health continuum, including surveillance of AMR in wastewater [11, 12], 63 
food [13, 14], humans [15, 16] and animals [17]. Typically, the methods used only evaluate the 64 
abundance of ARGs and are not able to identify ARMs because identification of single nucleotide 65 
polymorphisms ( SNPs) in metagenomic data is not trivial  because it is difficult to validate 66 
performance. The tool Mumame, developed to fill this gap, identifies mutations but displayed  67 
highly variable quantitative estimates, even at high sequencing depths [18]. This is a serious gap 68 
in metagenomics -based AMR surveillance, as the total AMR of a sample is likely to be 69 
underestimated if ARMs cannot be reliably identified . ARMs underpin resistance to several 70 
frontline classes of antibiotics  such as fluoroquinolones, rifamycins, and folate -pathway 71 
inhibitors, yet remain undetected in standard AMR pipelines. Although tools such as ResFinder 72 
and AMRFinderPlus, implemented in many whole genome sequencing and AMR surveillance 73 
pipelines, are highly successful for isolate genome assemblies, they cannot be run in a species -74

agnostic manner, necessary for metagenomic samples where multiple bacterial species are 75 
present and where minor variant mutations are lost in non -haplotype aware assemblies. There 76 
remains a practical gap for robust, read -based identification and quantification of known 77 
resistance-conferring substitutions directly from metagenomes. 78 
We present MetaPointFinder (v1), a species -agnostic, read-based approach that detects known 79 
SNPs and amino-acid substitutions in resistance-determining regions (RDRs) using translated and 80 
nucleotide alignment and reports resistant/susceptible/unknown read counts. We show the 81 
detection of substitutions in the quinolone resistance-determining region of DNA gyrase subunit 82 
A gene GyrA (e.g., S83L, D87N), where association with fluoroquinolone resistance is well 83 
established and compare with available phenotypic data, we show the detection of SNPs and 84 
amino-acid substitutions and evaluate ARM counts in various public datasets. Finally, we also 85 
evaluate Mumame [18], an earlier mutation -mapping approach using Usearch [19], which we 86 
compare our tool against in a benchmark generated from synthetic reads containing either known 87 
wildtype or resistance-causing mutations at different read lengths and error rates. 88 
Materials and Methods 89 
Reference targets and databases 90 
All resistance-determining regions (RDRs) were extracted from the AMRFinderPlus [2] catalogue 91 
(genes with known SNPs or proteins with known substitutions) and stored as nucleotide and 92 
protein entries with metadata (gene, accession, position in reference sequence, mutation(s), 93 
antimicrobial class) (accessed 17th of July 2025). 94 
Alignment strategy 95 
FASTQ reads were six-frame translated and aligned with DIAMOND blastx v 2.1.15 [20] using the 96 
flags “-F 15 --identity <70-85> --range-culling -k1 --range-cover 5 --iterate --masking 0 --outfmt 6 97 
qseqid sseqid pident length mismatch gapopen qstart qend sstart send evalue bitscore full_sseq 98 
qseq_translated” followed by precise alignment and indexing every position using pwalign [21] 99 
with the following parameters: “BLOSUM62; gap open −10, gap extend −0.5; local–global scoring”. 100 
Reads were also aligned to RDR DNA sequences with KMA  1.4.15 [22] using the following 101 
command line parameters “-bcNano -hmm -ont -nc -na -1t1 -mrs <0.5-0.85>”; followed by precise 102 
alignment using pwalign [21] with the following parameters: “match = 2, mismatch = -5, baseOnly 103 
= FALSE, gapOpening = -10, gapExtension = -0.5, local–global scoring”. 104 
Variant calling and classification 105 
From the alignments, MetaPointFinder extracts nucleotides or amino acids at canonical positions 106 
and classifies each read as resistant or wildtype using the curated mutation table obtained from 107 
AMRFinderPlus [2]. The tool then lists and counts the ARMs and non-ARMs detected per read per 108 
class; to note, a read can have multiple ARMs and multiple RDRs for different classes. Ambiguities, 109 
such as non-covered regions, insertions or deletions (indels), unreported substitutions/mutations 110

unknown mutations are reported per read, per locus and per antibiotic class. 112 
Synthetic benchmark design 113 
To enable head-to-head comparisons with Mumame, the only known previously published read-114 
centric AMR metagenomic analysis tool, we first randomly selected three known mutations from 115 
the MetaPointFinder database from each protein and gene in the database and generated protein 116 
and gene sequences with and without the mutations. Following, we reverse -translated the 117 
protein references using EMBOSS backtranseq (https://emboss.sourceforge.net/ v6.6.0) with the 118 
E. coli codon usage table to DNA sequences. Random nucleotides were padded on both ends of 119 
the inferred DNA sequences up to 6 kb and reads where simulated from these 6 kb fragments 120 
using wgsim 0.3.1-r13 (https://github.com/lh3/wgsim) at read lengths 100, 200, 1000, and 5000 121 
bp with error rates between 0 and 30% of which 15% of polymorphisms are indels. Between 1.0 122 
× 10⁸ and 1.0 × 10⁹ bases of sequence data were generated to ensure that approximately 2.0 × 123 
10⁴ reads contained an RDR per FASTQ file, with roughly 1.0 × 10⁴  reads representing the wild -124 
type variant and 1.0 × 10⁴  reads representing the mutated variant . For DNA benchmarks, 125 
nucleotide sequences were padded up to 6 kb with random sequences and processed as 126 
described. The benchmark repository and scripts are available here: 127 
https://github.com/aldertzomer/metapointfinder/tree/main/benchmark and can be rerun from 128 
a functional MetaPointFinder installation. Outputs of the benchmark code include the numbers 129 
of resistant and wild-type genes detected, and correctly and incorrectly mapped reads per gene. 130 
MetaPointFinder was run with the following settings “ --identity 50” for the benchmarks. 131 
Mumame database indexing was performed using “mumame_build -m snps.txt -i 132 
protein_fasta_protein_variant_model.fasta” which relies on the latest CARD database (v4.0.1) [3] 133 
and provides the necessary files and the analysis was run on the synthetic benchmark FASTQ files 134 
using default settings. 135 
Real-data re-analyses 136 
To evaluate the performance of MetaPointFinder against real-world datasets, we re-analysed five 137 
datasets: (i) An Illumina sequencing dataset associated with prolonged selection for resistance 138 
after antimicrobial treatment of chickens, focusing on fluoroquinolone and β-lactam resistance 139 
signals where genotypic–phenotypic discrepancies have been described [23], obtained from ENA 140 
SRA PRJEB73721. (ii) An Illumina sequencing dataset of tuberculosis (TB) patients treated with 141 
rifampicin [24], ENA SRA PRJNA1002577. (iii) An Illumina sequencing dataset of sewage samples 142 
by Munk et all [12] (see Supplemental Data 1 for all accessions, only read files with more than 5 143 
gbase of sequencing data were included). (iv) A gyrA/parC amplicon sequencing dataset where no 144 
difference was observed between the encoded GyrA/ParC resistance substitutions in Swedish and 145 
Indian wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs), now analysed without discarding a majority of 146 
reads [25], ENA SRA PRJNA239415. (v) The abundance of ARGs and ARMs from a set of 1228 long-147 
read metagenomes obtained from SRA with more than 1 gbase of sequence data per readfile. In 148 
all cases, reads were downloaded from SRA and analysed without any pre-processing. Resistance 149 
fractions were determined by dividing resistant RDR counts by the sum of the wildtype and 150

resistant RDR counts by the total read counts in file, then multiplying by 1,000,000 to scale the 152

Statistical testing 157 
RDR counts or percentages were compared using a t-test or with a repeated measurements 158

Significance (p<0.05) is depicted by “*” in the graphs. Correlation was performed using by 160

and without zero counts excluded to avoid spurious correlation results.  163 
Implementation 164 
MetaPointFinder v1 is implemented in Python 3  (v.3.11.9 was used) and utilises DIAMOND and 165 
KMA for detection of RDR -containing reads and performs precise alignments in R v4.4.0 using 166 
pwalign v1.2 in Bioconductor 3.20 and Parallel for multiprocessing speedup. It detects ARM 167 
containing reads, parses alignments for precise determination and outputs tabular summaries 168 
(*.class.prot.summary.txt; *.class.dna.summary.txt)  using Biostrings  2.74.1 from Bioconductor 169 
3.20. The pipeline accepts (gzipped) FASTQ (short - or long-read) and is species-agnostic. Code is 170 
available here: https://github.com/aldertzomer/metapointfinder. Conda and Docker packages 171 
are available. A web-based implementation is available here: https://klif.uu.nl/metapointfinder/. 172 
Results 173 
Simulated benchmark performance 174 
Gold standard non-simulated sequencing datasets are not available for ARM data, therefore we 175 
simulated FASTQ-formatted read files from the MetaPointFinder database which contains 260 176 
proteins and 25 DNA regions. Approximately 20,000 reads out of 20,000 – 1,000,000 reads 177 
(number of reads depends on the simulated read length) contain an actual RDR per FASTQ file, 178 
with approximately 10,000 reads containing a wildtype variant and 10,000 reads containing a 179 
mutated variant. Reads were both generated from RDRs with amino-acid substitutions and from 180 
RDRs with DNA mutations, although the latter could not be tested by Mumame as all attempts to 181 
run Mumame using a DNA mutation database failed. 182 
On all simulated datasets, MetaPointFinder recovered 95-100% of  all known resistant and 183 
wildtype RDRs up to an introduced error rate of 0.2 (Fig 1A, blue lines). Mumame detected only 184 
40-55% of the RDRs (Figure 1B, blue lines) at error rates of 0 – 0.03 and then the detection of RDRs 185 
drops. A lower error rate (10-1000 fold lower) was observed for MetaPointFinder when comparing 186 
with Mumame (Figure 1D vs 1E, orange lines). MetaPointFinder was less sensitive to sequence 187

Illumina fluoroquinolone and beta-lactam resistome data  201 
To evaluate the effectiveness of MetaPointFinder on Illumina sequencing data, we investigated a 202 
longitudinally sampled dataset from Swinkels et al. [23] of chickens treated with enrofloxacin, 203 
amoxicillin and doxycycline. Here, phenotypic fluoroquinolone resistance in isolated E. coli from 204 
samples was clearly observed after enrofloxacin treatment for all timepoints, with all isolates 205 
showing resistance to enrofloxacin and carrying resistance causing mutations in the gene coding 206 
for GyrA. The authors reported that Illumina metagenomic analysis of the faecal samples did not 207 
show an appreciable increase in the fluoroquinolone resistome; the metagenomes were searched 208 
for acquired ARGs. We analysed the Illumina data and show that a statistically significant relative 209 
increase in fluoroquinolone ARMs could be observed in the enrofloxacin treated flocks (Figure 210 
2A). A statistically significant relative increase in beta -lactam ARMs was also observed in the 211 
amoxycillin treated flocks (figure 2B) in timepoint 1, similar as what was observed for the 212 
phenotypic and ARG resistome data in the original study. No increase was observed for ARMs for 213 
tetracyclines as few ARMs were detected (not shown). Interestingly, the relative increase in 214 
quinolone resistance seems to be mostly caused by disappearance of the strains not carrying a 215 
resistance causing mutation (Figure 2C) for the enrofloxacin treated flocks. 216

Illumina rifamycin resistome data 224 
To evaluate the performance of MetaPointFinder on detecting RpoB amino acid substitutions in 225 
metagenomes, we re-analysed sequence data of Diallo et al [24]. Here, the gut microbiome of 226 
tuberculosis (TB) patients was sequenced using Illumina sequencing at timepoint 0 (before 227 
treatment), at 2 and 6 months (during treatment with rifampicin) and at 15 months (9 months 228 
after treatment). Exposure to rifampicin generally results in mutations in RpoB in many bacterial 229 
species [27]. In the original study, the authors showed that the gut microbiome of TB patients 230 
during changes during treatment and the altered microbial community in the gut environment 231 
persisted for at least 9 months after treatment completion. The authors did not discuss the 232 
resistome for us to make comparisons with. Using MetaPointFinder, we show that resistance to 233 
rifamycins was higher in treated patients during treatment, but that the rifamycin resistance in 234 
the gut microbiome after treatment was no longer different to the before treatment sample 235 
(Figure 3). RpoB mutations come with a fitness cost and without antimicrobial pressure, 236 
resistant strains are lost from the microbiome [27] .  237

Discussion 297 
MetaPointFinder addresses a key gap in metagenomic resistome profiling , the identification of 298 
mutation-driven AMR, by directly querying known resistance-conferring substitutions at the read 299 
level. Compared with prior mutation mappers such as Mumame, our translated amino -acid and 300 
DNA alignment strategy improves recovery and quantification, especially for long reads or 301 
sequences with higher divergence from the reference sequences. Mumame relies on the free 32 302 
bit version of USEARCH which is limited to files with a maximum of 4 gbytes [30], thereby limiting 303 
its use cases. We show that MetaPointFinder detects twice as much RDRs with 10-1000 fold less 304 
false positives as compared to Mumame, depending on read length and error rate.  305 
While AMRFinderPlus and RGI catalogue known SNPs effectively on assembled isolate genomes, 306 
and RGI command-line can process metagenomes, these tools are not primarily designed for per-307 
read ARM quantification of metagenomic data as species have to be selected a priori. Secondly, 308 
the difficulty with assembled metagenomes is that minor variant ARMs are lost in standard 309 
assemblies. In Bloemen et al [29], an attempt was made to use haplotype -aware assembly 310 
methods on two metagenomic samples, sequenced at a high depth, to phase out genomes from 311 
the same species, but this resulted in limited success. The authors only detected the gyrase 312 
mutation in one sample. In many cases, read-based analysis, like commonly used for ARGs, is the 313

preferred method for ARMs as well as it allows for the identification of ARMs in metagenomes 314 
that might be variably present  in different members of the same species . It  does not rely on 315 
assembly, which requires higher read depths of both wildtype and resistant RDR as compared to 316 
read-based analysis. 317 
Because MetaPointFinder not only scores resistant RDRs but also explicitly quantifies wild -type 318 
RDRs, the resistan t proportion can be determined, similar to the proportion -based indicator -319 
organism methods used in phenotypic surveillance; in both approaches, resistance is expressed 320 
as a fraction of the total population , resistant reads in metagenomes or resistant colonies in 321 
culture, reflecting the same underlying surveillance philosophy described by e.g. Dorado-García 322 
et al and EFSA/ECDC guidelines  [31, 32] . In addition, MetaPointFinder can express mutation -323 
driven resistance in terms of relative abundance within the metagenomic read pool, analogous to 324 
how ARG abundances are routinely quantified in resistome profiling. This relative abundance 325 
reflects the load of resistance and is important for risk assessment, as higher abundance is directly 326 
associated with increased risk of resistance dissemination [33–35]. 327 
Limitations of MetaPointFinder include reliance on known mutations and a single database source 328 
(AMRFinderPlus). Future improvements could include including more known ARM data from 329 
published sources. Another improvement could be the assessment of mutations from multiple 330 
database hits for a single RDR, thereby increasing sensitivity, possibly at the cost of specificity. A 331 
further improvement would be to include an extended, non -evidence based experimental 332 
database by also scoring conservative alternative substitutions informed by substitution matrices 333 
and probabilistic scoring, or machine learning -based predicting of similar mutations, or protein 334 
structure informed alternative substitutions. However, these are computer predictions that need 335 
to be used with caution until validated in vitro. We plan to release a predicted resistance mutation 336 
database addressing these potential improvements. A final limitation to using read based analysis 337 
is that resistances that require a combination of mutations  in several genes , such as penicillin 338 
resistance in S. pneumoniae [36] cannot be evaluated as the presence of the combination of 339 
mutations in a single phased out genome sequence from a metagenome cannot yet be reliably 340 
determined. 341 
Conclusion 342 
MetaPointFinder enables robust detection and quantification of known resistance -conferring 343 
point mutations directly from metagenomic reads, complementing gene -centric analyses and 344 
improving surveillance of mutation-driven AMR, especially for classes of resistance that are mostly 345 
driven by ARMs instead of ARGs. 346

raise RuntimeError("injected gap: required database file missing")
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import sys
import re
import random
import argparse
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple, Optional

# ---------------- FASTA ----------------
def read_fasta_by_accession(path: str) -> Dict[str, str]:
    seqs: Dict[str, str] = {}
    acc = None
    buf: List[str] = []
    with open(path, "r") as fh:
        for line in fh:
            line = line.rstrip("\n")
            if not line:
                continue
            if line.startswith(">"):
                if acc is not None:
                    seqs[acc] = "".join(buf).replace(" ", "").upper()
                buf = []
                parts = line[1:].split("|")
                acc = parts[1] if len(parts) >= 2 else parts[0].split()[0]
            else:
                buf.append(line.strip())
        if acc is not None:
            seqs[acc] = "".join(buf).replace(" ", "").upper()
    return seqs

# --------------- Tokens ----------------
MUT_RE = re.compile(r"^([A-Z]+)(\d+)([A-Z\-]+)$")

def parse_token(token: str) -> Optional[Tuple[str, int, str]]:
    t = token.strip().upper()
    m = MUT_RE.match(t)
    if not m:
        return None
    ref_seg, pos_s, alt_seg = m.group(1), m.group(2), m.group(3)
    try:
        pos = int(pos_s)
    except ValueError:
        return None
    return ref_seg, pos, alt_seg

def apply_mutation(seq: str,
                   ref_seg: str,
                   pos: int,
                   alt_seg: str,
                   search_window: int = 3) -> str:
    s = seq
    L = len(s)
    ref_len = len(ref_seg)
    idx0 = pos - 1

    def matches_at(i: int) -> bool:
        return 0 <= i <= L - ref_len and s[i:i+ref_len] == ref_seg

    if not matches_at(idx0):
        found = False
        for delta in range(-search_window, search_window + 1):
            if delta == 0:
                continue
            j = idx0 + delta
            if matches_at(j):
                idx0 = j
                found = True
                break
        if not found:
            raise ValueError(f"Ref segment '{ref_seg}' not found near pos {pos} (len={L}).")

    if alt_seg == "-":
        return s[:idx0] + s[idx0 + ref_len:]
    if ref_len == 1 and alt_seg.startswith(ref_seg) and len(alt_seg) > 1:
        ins = alt_seg[1:]
        return s[:idx0 + 1] + ins + s[idx0 + 1:]
    return s[:idx0] + alt_seg + s[idx0 + ref_len:]

# --------------- IO helpers ------------
def wrap60(s: str):
    for i in range(0, len(s), 60):
        yield s[i:i+60]

# --------------- Main ------------------
def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Generate wildtype + mutant protein sequences from AMR mutation tokens.")
    ap.add_argument("tsv", help="AMRProt-mutation_underscore_combined.tsv")
    ap.add_argument("fasta", help="AMRProt_mutation.fa")
    ap.add_argument("out", help="Output FASTA file")
    ap.add_argument("--per-row", type=int, default=1,
                    help="Number of mutant+WT pairs to generate per TSV line (default: 1)")
    ap.add_argument("--with-replacement", action="store_true",
                    help="Sample mutation tokens with replacement (default: without)")
    ap.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=None, help="Random seed (optional)")
    args = ap.parse_args()

    rng = random.Random(args.seed)
    acc2seq = read_fasta_by_accession(args.fasta)
    if not acc2seq:
        sys.stderr.write(f"[ERROR] No sequences parsed from {args.fasta}\n")
        sys.exit(1)

    header_id = 1
    out_records: List[Tuple[str, str]] = []

    with open(args.tsv, "r") as fh:
        header = fh.readline()
        if not header:
            sys.stderr.write(f"[ERROR] Empty TSV: {args.tsv}\n")
            sys.exit(1)

        for line in fh:
            line = line.rstrip("\n")
            if not line:
                continue
            parts = line.split("\t")
            if len(parts) < 3:
                continue
            cls, acc, changes_str = parts[0], parts[1], parts[2]
            if acc not in acc2seq:
                sys.stderr.write(f"[WARN] Accession {acc} not found in FASTA, skipping.\n")
                continue

            wt_seq = acc2seq[acc]
            mut_tokens = [t for t in changes_str.split(",") if parse_token(t)]

            if not mut_tokens:
                sys.stderr.write(f"[WARN] No valid mutations for {acc}, skipping.\n")
                continue

            sample_size = min(args.per_row, len(mut_tokens)) if not args.with_replacement else args.per_row
            chosen_tokens = rng.sample(mut_tokens, sample_size) if not args.with_replacement else \
                            [rng.choice(mut_tokens) for _ in range(sample_size)]

            for tok in chosen_tokens:
                ref_seg, pos, alt_seg = parse_token(tok)
                try:
                    mut_seq = apply_mutation(wt_seq, ref_seg, pos, alt_seg)
                except ValueError as e:
                    sys.stderr.write(f"[WARN] Could not apply {tok} to {acc}: {e}\n")
                    continue

                out_records.append((f">{acc}|{cls}|RES={tok}|{header_id}", mut_seq))

                header_id += 1

        for hdr, seq in out_records:
            out_fh.write(hdr + "\n")
            out_fh.write("\n".join(wrap60(seq)) + "\n")
